title: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
summary: Why neurons are polysemantic, how sparse autoencoders recover feature directions, how to train, read and evaluate them, where they fall short, and how to train one on GPT-2.
outcomes: Explain superposition and why sparsity lets a layer hold more features than dimensions
Write the SAE encoder, decoder and loss, and explain why decoder norms enter the sparsity penalty
Explain L1 shrinkage and how TopK, Gated and JumpReLU SAEs avoid it, including how a JumpReLU threshold is trained
Diagnose dead latents and feature splitting, and choose fixes such as AuxK and resampling
Name a latent from its activating examples and logit effect, and score an explanation by simulation or detection
Compute L0, FVU and loss recovered under zero or mean ablation, and steer a model by clamping a latent
Explain feature absorption and decide when a linear probe or difference-in-means beats an SAE
Train a TopK SAE on GPT-2 activations, and load, read and steer with a released SAE

lessons.title: Why single neurons are hard to read: superposition

blocks.md:
In the GPT you built, every token carries a vector through the network: the residual stream, whose width `d_model` is the number of entries in that vector (768 in GPT-2 small, where nanoGPT calls it `n_embd`), and inside each block an MLP layer with a few thousand neurons. Interpretability asks what those numbers mean. The obvious plan is to read neurons one at a time: find the inputs that make neuron 227 fire and give it a name.

That plan mostly fails in language models. Many neurons are **polysemantic**: they fire for several unrelated things. The opposite, a neuron that fires for one clean, nameable thing, would be **monosemantic** (from Greek: poly means many, mono means one, and semantic means meaning). In Anthropic's one-layer transformer, the neuron most correlated with a clean DNA-sequence feature had DNA as only a tiny sliver of its top activating examples.

blocks.caption: An activation vector x is a bias plus a sum of feature directions d_i, each scaled by how strongly feature i is present. Most f_i are zero on any given token.

blocks.md: Why can a $d$-dimensional space hold more than $d$ useful directions? Only $d$ vectors can be exactly orthogonal, but in high dimensions random directions are **almost** orthogonal. The **cosine** of two unit vectors is their dot product: 1 when they point the same way, 0 when they are orthogonal. Here is why random directions overlap so little. Rotate the space so the first vector lies on the first axis; the cosine is then just the second vector's first coordinate $v_1$. A unit vector has $v_1^2 + v_2^2 + \dots + v_d^2 = 1$, and for a random direction every coordinate is alike by symmetry, so each squared coordinate averages $1/d$. So for two random unit vectors in $d$ dimensions the mean squared cosine is exactly $1/d$, and the typical size of the cosine, its **root mean square** (the square root of the mean of the squares), is $1/\sqrt{d}$. For $d = 768$ that is $1/27.7$, about 0.036. The overlap between two feature directions is called **interference**: when one feature fires, every overlapping feature looks slightly active too.

blocks.title: Typical overlap between random directions shrinks with width

y.label: RMS cosine of two random unit vectors

scenes.caption: The curve is the exact RMS cosine 1/sqrt(d). Dots are a simulation with 2,000 random pairs per width; they sit on the curve.
At d = 2 two random directions overlap heavily (about 0.7). At GPT-2 small's width of 768 the typical overlap is about 0.035, so many nearly independent directions fit.

blocks.md:
Toy Models makes this concrete with a tiny network. Five features $x_1..x_5$ (each zero with high probability, otherwise uniform in $[0,1]$) are squeezed into a 2-dimensional hidden vector and decoded back:

$h = Wx$, then $x' = \text{ReLU}(W^T h + b)$.

The **ReLU** (rectified linear unit) is $\max(z, 0)$: it passes positive values and turns negative ones into 0. $b$ is a bias added to every output before it. $W$ is a 2 by 5 matrix whose columns are the feature directions, so $h$ is the sum of the active features' directions, and decoding computes $W^T h = W^T W x$. Entry $(i, j)$ of $W^T W$ is the dot product of directions $i$ and $j$, which for unit vectors is their cosine: it says how much feature $j$ leaks into output $i$. When the features are sparse, the paper's trained models place the five directions on a **pentagon**. Below we use a hand-built pentagon (unit vectors 72 degrees apart, since 360 divided by 5 is 72) so every number can be checked. Neighbours meet at 72 degrees, cosine 0.309; non-neighbours at 144 degrees, cosine -0.809. We set $b = -0.309$ on every output, exactly the size of a neighbour's leak, so that the leaks of a lone feature cancel to zero.

blocks.title: Interference matrix W-transpose W for five features on a pentagon

scenes.caption: Entry (i, j) is the cosine between directions i and j. The diagonal is 1: each feature reads itself back perfectly.
Neighbours on the pentagon overlap by +0.309 (cos 72 degrees). This is positive interference: f1 firing makes f2 and f5 look slightly on.
Non-neighbours overlap by -0.809. Negative interference is harmless here because the output ReLU clips negative values to zero.

blocks.title: Decoding the pentagon with bias b = -0.309 and a ReLU

scenes.caption: Only f1 is on (value 1). Before the ReLU the output is W-transpose W x: f1 reads 1.0, but f2 and f5 leak +0.309. f3 and f4 read -0.809: bar height shows size, the label shows the sign.
Adding b = -0.309 and applying the ReLU wipes out the leak. f1 comes back as 0.691: a bit shrunk, but no false features.
f1 and its neighbour f2 both on. Pre-activations are 1.309 and 1.309; after the bias both read exactly 1.0. Adjacent pairs decode cleanly.
f1 and f3 both on. Pre-activations are 0.191, 0.618, 0.191: after the bias the true features vanish and f2, which is off, reads 0.309. Interference wins.

blocks.prompt: If each of the five features is independently active with probability p, how often do two or more fire at once (the case that can break the pentagon)? Guess for p = 0.5 and p = 0.05.
blocks.reveal:
Count the complement. No feature fires with probability $(1-p)^5$. Exactly one fires with probability $5p(1-p)^4$: 5 choices for which one, it is on, and the other 4 are off. Two or more is everything else, $1-(1-p)^5-5p(1-p)^4$:

- p = 0.5: 81% of inputs have two or more features on, so superposition is costly.
- p = 0.1: 8.1%.
- p = 0.05: 2.3%.
- p = 0.01: 0.1%.

Sparsity makes collisions rare, which is why Toy Models finds that sparse features get stored in superposition while dense ones (active on many inputs) get a dedicated orthogonal dimension or are dropped.

blocks.md:
Toy Models reports a **phase change**: as sparsity rises, a feature switches from not represented, to represented in superposition, to (if important enough) represented on its own dimension. In the paper's version where the five features differ in importance, dense features get an orthogonal basis for only the two most important ones, much like **PCA** (principal component analysis, which keeps the few orthogonal directions along which the data varies most).

The consequence for interpretability: if a real model works this way, its neurons are the wrong unit of analysis. We need a method that finds the feature directions themselves. That is what a sparse autoencoder does.

You can watch this happen in a few seconds of CPU time. Train the toy above with five features in two dimensions, importances $I_i = 0.7^i$ (the decay the paper uses for its 20-feature version), and the loss $\sum_i I_i (x_i - x'_i)^2$, once per sparsity level, keeping the best of three seeds. The bars below show the length $\|W_i\|$ of each feature's direction: about 1 means the feature is represented, 0 means it was dropped. Our run used 10,000 Adam steps of 1,024 samples each; the paper trains similar models and finds the same progression.

blocks.title: Five features in two dimensions: feature norms as sparsity rises

scenes.caption: Dense features (every feature nonzero on every input). The two most important features get orthogonal directions of length 1; the other three are dropped. This is the PCA-like solution.

Density 0.3 (each feature nonzero 30% of the time). Four features are now represented in two dimensions: superposition. Each overlaps fully with one partner, the antipodal pairs the paper describes. The least important is still dropped.
Density 0.1: the same four-feature arrangement, with lower loss because collisions are rarer.
Density 0.03: all five features are represented, each overlapping with others. The phase change: the fifth feature jumped from not represented to in superposition.
Density 0.001: five features in two dimensions, the pentagon regime of the figures above. In this run the lengths settle a little above 1.

blocks.md: Superposition: a layer with $d$ dimensions can represent many more than $d$ sparse features as almost-orthogonal directions, at the cost of interference. Neurons then mix many features, so we look for directions instead.

Superposition is a hypothesis with strong toy-model evidence, not a proven fact about every layer of every LLM. The pentagon above is hand-built for clean numbers; trained toy models find it too, but their exact weights and biases differ.

blocks.question: A colleague says: 'If a model had 768 dimensions, it could track at most 768 features without errors, so superposition can't help.' What is the best reply?
options: Exact orthogonality caps it at 768, but many sparse features can share almost-orthogonal directions because they rarely fire together, and a ReLU filters small interference.
Right: superposition only works when features are dense and frequently co-occur.
Wrong: 768 dimensions can hold 768 squared exactly orthogonal directions.
Right: that is why language models need one neuron per feature.
blocks.explain: Only d directions can be exactly orthogonal, but random directions in 768 dimensions overlap by only about 0.036. When features are sparse, two overlapping features are rarely on together, and a negative bias plus ReLU removes the small leaks. Dense features make collisions common, which is when superposition stops paying.

blocks.question: In the pentagon model, which input is decoded wrongly with b = -0.309?
options: Only f1 on
f1 and f2 on (neighbours)
f1 and f3 on (non-neighbours)
No feature on
blocks.explain: Non-neighbours have cosine -0.809, so their sum cancels most of each one's own signal (0.191 each) while the shared neighbour f2 gets 0.618. After the bias only f2 survives. Neighbours reinforce each other instead.

lessons.title: The sparse autoencoder: a wide, sparse dictionary for activations

blocks.md: An **autoencoder** is a network trained to reproduce its own input: an **encoder** maps the input to a hidden code, a **decoder** maps the code back, and the loss measures how far the output lands from the input. A **sparse autoencoder (SAE)** is a separate, small network trained to rewrite one layer's activations as a sparse sum of learned directions. The language model stays frozen. You run it over a large text corpus, save the activation vector $\mathbf{x}$ at one site (an MLP output, or the residual stream at some layer) for every token, then train the SAE on those vectors.

The SAE has one hidden layer that is much **wider** than $\mathbf{x}$: $M \gg d$ hidden units called **latents**, where $d$ is the width of $\mathbf{x}$. Each latent owns one decoder column, its dictionary direction. The word comes from **dictionary learning**, a classic signal-processing method that writes every data vector as a sparse combination of a learned set of vectors called the dictionary. A sparsity penalty makes only a handful of latents fire per token, which is exactly the superposition picture from lesson 1 run in reverse.

The form below comes from Anthropic's 2023 paper *Towards Monosemanticity* (Bricken et al.), which trained SAEs on a one-layer transformer. Its 2024 follow-up, *Scaling Monosemanticity* (Templeton et al.), scaled them up to Claude 3 Sonnet, one of Anthropic's production models.

blocks.caption: Encoder: subtract a learned centre b_dec, multiply by an M by d matrix W_enc, add a bias b_enc, then ReLU, giving latents f. Decoder: multiply by W_dec and add b_dec back. Column i of W_dec (written d_i) is latent i's direction, so x-hat is b_dec plus the sum of f_i times d_i.

blocks.title: Where the SAE sits and what it computes

scenes.caption: Activations are collected from a frozen model, token by token. Towards Monosemanticity used 8 billion MLP activation vectors from a one-layer transformer.
The encoder projects x into M latents, many more than d. The ReLU zeroes every latent whose pre-activation is negative.
The decoder adds up the directions of the active latents. Few latents fire, so x-hat is a sparse combination of dictionary vectors.
Training pushes two ways: reconstruct x well (MSE) and keep f sparse. The tension between them is the whole design problem of the next lesson.

blocks.md: The loss has two terms. The first is the squared reconstruction error $\|\mathbf{x}-\hat{\mathbf{x}}\|_2^2$, the squared straight-line (L2) length of the difference; averaged over tokens it is the mean squared error. The second is a sparsity penalty built on the **L1 norm**, the sum of absolute values $\sum_i |f_i|$. After a ReLU every $f_i$ is at least 0, so it is simply the sum of the latent activations. Charging $\lambda$ for every unit of activation makes it cheaper to leave a latent at exactly 0 than to use it a little, which is what keeps most latents off.

blocks.caption: The L1-style loss from Scaling Monosemanticity. In words: averaged over tokens, the squared reconstruction error plus lambda times the sum of each latent's activation times the length of its decoder column. lambda sets the trade-off: larger lambda gives fewer active latents and worse reconstruction.

blocks.md:
Why multiply each $f_i$ by its decoder norm $\|\mathbf{d}_i\|$? Without it the SAE can cheat: halve every $f_i$ and double every $\mathbf{d}_i$, and the reconstruction is unchanged while the penalty halves. Towards Monosemanticity blocked this by forcing decoder columns to unit norm; Scaling Monosemanticity instead puts the norm inside the penalty and reports $f_i \|\mathbf{d}_i\|$ as the feature activation.

**Worked example.** Take the pentagon from lesson 1 as a ready-made dictionary: five unit decoder columns in $d = 2$, encoder rows equal to the same directions (tied weights, as in Cunningham et al., a 2023 paper that trained SAEs on open language models), $\mathbf{b}_{dec} = 0$, $\mathbf{b}_{enc} = -0.309$. Feed it the activation produced by feature 1 at strength 0.8: $\mathbf{x} = (0.8, 0)$.

blocks.title: One activation through a 5-latent SAE (d = 2)

scenes.caption: Input: the 2-d activation (0.8, 0). Five latents, one per pentagon direction.
Encoder pre-activations are dot products with each direction: 0.8 for latent 0, and interference of 0.247 on its two neighbours.
Add b_enc = -0.309 and ReLU: neighbours drop below zero and switch off. Only latent 0 fires (L0, the count of active latents, is 1), but at 0.491 instead of 0.8.
Decode: x-hat = 0.491 times direction 0 = (0.491, 0). Squared error is 0.309 squared = 0.095. The right latent fired, but it was shrunk.

blocks.prompt: The bias that silenced the false latents also shrank the true one by exactly 0.309. Is that a coincidence of this example, or a general problem with 'ReLU plus a negative bias' as a way to get sparsity?
blocks.reveal: It is general. A ReLU with bias $b$ subtracts the same amount from every active latent, so the one knob both filters noise and biases the magnitude down. Real L1-trained SAEs show the same effect, called **shrinkage**. Lesson 3 shows how TopK and JumpReLU separate 'which latents fire' from 'how big they are'.

blocks.code:
import torch, torch.nn as nn

class SAE(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d, M):
        super().__init__()
        self.W_enc = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(M, d) * 0.01)
        self.b_enc = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(M))
        self.W_dec = nn.Parameter(self.W_enc.data.T.clone())  # init dec = enc^T
        self.b_dec = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(d))

    def forward(self, x):                      # x: [batch, d]
        f = torch.relu((x - self.b_dec) @ self.W_enc.T + self.b_enc)
        x_hat = f @ self.W_dec.T + self.b_dec  # [batch, d]
        return f, x_hat

def sae_loss(sae, x, lam):
    f, x_hat = sae(x)
    mse = ((x - x_hat) ** 2).sum(-1).mean()
    dec_norms = sae.W_dec.norm(dim=0)          # one norm per latent
    sparsity = (f * dec_norms).sum(-1).mean()
    return mse + lam * sparsity
blocks.caption: A minimal L1 SAE in PyTorch following the equations above. Real training adds activation normalisation, large batches and dead-latent handling; lesson 8 builds all three on GPT-2.

blocks.md:
Sizes in published work:

- **Towards Monosemanticity** (Anthropic, 2023): a 512-neuron MLP in a one-layer transformer, dictionaries from 512 (1x) to 131,072 (256x) latents.
- **Cunningham et al.** (2023): residual streams of Pythia-70M and Pythia-410M (EleutherAI's open models with 70 million and 410 million parameters).
- **Scaling Monosemanticity** (Anthropic, 2024): the middle-layer residual stream of Claude 3 Sonnet, with about 1 million, 4 million and 34 million latents.
- **Scaling and evaluating SAEs** (OpenAI, 2024, Gao et al.): 16 million latents on GPT-4, trained on 40 billion tokens.
- **Gemma Scope** (Google DeepMind, 2024): more than 400 open SAEs covering every layer and sublayer of Gemma 2 2B and 9B (Google's open models with 2 and 9 billion parameters), with over 30 million latents in total.

An SAE is dictionary learning with a neural network: an encoder that picks a few latents, a decoder whose columns are the dictionary directions, and a loss that trades reconstruction against sparsity.

Words to keep apart: a **latent** is a unit of the SAE; a **feature** is the concept you hope it captures. Gemma Scope says 'latents' for exactly this reason. A latent with a clean name is a hypothesis about a model feature, not proof of one. Lesson 5 shows how a latent gets its name and how that name is tested.

blocks.question: Why does Scaling Monosemanticity multiply each latent's activation by its decoder norm inside the sparsity penalty?
options: To make the encoder run faster
So the SAE cannot lower the penalty by shrinking activations while growing decoder columns, which would leave reconstructions unchanged
To force exactly k latents to be active
Because decoder norms equal the language model's loss
blocks.explain: Scaling f_i down by c and d_i up by c leaves f_i d_i (and so x-hat) unchanged but cuts a plain L1 penalty by c. Weighting by the decoder norm makes the penalty invariant to that rescaling. A unit-norm constraint on decoder columns achieves the same thing.

blocks.question: You train an SAE on layer 6 residual-stream activations of your GPT. Which statement is true?
options: The GPT's weights are updated so its neurons become monosemantic
The SAE has fewer hidden units than d_model so it compresses the activations
The SAE is trained on next-token cross-entropy only
The GPT is frozen; the SAE learns a wider, sparse re-description of the saved layer 6 vectors
blocks.explain: The SAE is a separate model trained on stored activations. It is overcomplete (M much larger than d) and trained with a reconstruction plus sparsity objective, not by changing the language model.

lessons.title: Enforcing sparsity: L1, TopK and JumpReLU

blocks.md:
What we really want to penalise is the number of active latents, the **L0 norm** $\|\mathbf{f}\|_0$. The name comes from the family of norms $\sum_i |f_i|^p$: as $p$ shrinks toward 0, every nonzero entry contributes 1 and every zero contributes 0, so what is left is a count (strictly it is not a norm, but the name stuck). A count only changes in jumps, when a latent crosses zero, so nudging the weights a little leaves it flat: it has zero gradient almost everywhere and cannot be trained directly with plain backprop. The first SAEs used the **L1 norm** from lesson 2, $\sum_i |f_i|$, as a differentiable stand-in.

L1 has a side effect. It charges for **size**, not just for being on, so the optimiser pays to make every active latent a little smaller than the data wants. This is **shrinkage**: systematic underestimation of feature activations (discussed in DeepMind's Gated SAE paper, covered below, and by Wright and Sharkey).

blocks.caption: One latent, unit decoder direction, true strength a. Loss: (a minus f) squared plus lambda f. Setting its derivative, minus 2 times (a minus f) plus lambda, to zero gives f = a minus lambda/2, or 0 if that is negative. So the L1 optimum is always lambda/2 short of the truth.

blocks.title: Shrinkage: the L1 optimum sits lambda/2 below the true activation

scenes.caption: With lambda = 0 both curves coincide and the best f equals a = 0.8. No sparsity pressure, no bias.
lambda = 0.3: the minimum moves to f = 0.65. The reconstruction error 0.15 squared = 0.023 is paid on every token where this latent fires.
lambda = 0.6: f = 0.5, error 0.09. Raising lambda buys sparsity (weak latents switch off entirely) but shrinks every surviving one.

blocks.md: **TopK SAEs** (Gao et al., OpenAI 2024, building on k-sparse autoencoders by Makhzani and Frey) drop the penalty. The encoder keeps only the $k$ largest pre-activations and zeroes the rest; the loss is reconstruction MSE alone. Benefits reported in the paper: no L1 shrinkage, L0 is set directly instead of tuned through $\lambda$, a better sparsity versus reconstruction frontier (the best reconstruction error reachable at each L0) than ReLU SAEs that widens with scale, and small noisy activations are clipped to zero.

blocks.caption: b_pre is a learned centre, subtracted before encoding and added back after decoding, like b_dec in lesson 2. TopK keeps the k largest pre-activations and zeroes the rest, giving z. The loss is only the squared reconstruction error: k already fixes how many latents fire.

blocks.title: TopK on the pentagon SAE: choosing k

scenes.caption: Same input as lesson 2, x = (0.8, 0), same tied pentagon SAE but no bias. Pre-activations: 0.8 on latent 0, 0.247 leaks on latents 1 and 4.
k = 1 keeps 0.8 untouched. x-hat = (0.8, 0) exactly: squared error 0. No shrinkage, because nothing taxes the magnitude.
k = 2 also keeps a leak (0.247, tie broken toward latent 1). x-hat = (0.876, 0.235), error 0.061. Too large a k admits interference.
New input with two true features: x = 0.8 d0 + 0.6 d1 = (0.985, 0.571). Pre-activations 0.985, 0.847, -0.462, -1.133, -0.238.
k = 1 keeps only latent 0: x-hat = (0.985, 0), error 0.326. A fixed k cannot adapt when a token genuinely has more features.

blocks.prompt: In the last scene, k = 2 would keep both correct latents, at 0.985 and 0.847. The true strengths are 0.8 and 0.6. Will reconstruction be perfect?
blocks.reveal: No. x-hat = (1.247, 0.806), squared error 0.124. The tied encoder reads each latent with a plain dot product, so the +0.309 overlap between neighbours inflates both readings. Re-fitting the two magnitudes by least squares on the chosen support (the set of latents that fired) gives exactly 0.8 and 0.6. Trained encoders learn rows that partly cancel such interference, and Gao et al. use this kind of refinement to measure leftover bias. Simplified: a real SAE's encoder is learned, not tied to the decoder.

blocks.md: **Gated SAEs** (Rajamanoharan et al., DeepMind 2024) split the encoder into a **gate path** that decides which latents are on and a **magnitude path** that sets their size. Both read the same centred input $\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b}_{dec}$. The gate is a Heaviside step (1 if its pre-activation is positive, else 0); the magnitude is a ReLU. To avoid doubling the encoder, the magnitude weights reuse the gate's directions, each row rescaled by a learned factor $e^{r_i}$, with separate biases. They report needing about half as many firing latents for the same reconstruction fidelity, at up to 50% more training compute per step.

blocks.caption: The gated encoder. pi_gate is the gate's pre-activation; the indicator 1[...] is 1 where it is positive; the circled dot multiplies elementwise. The magnitude path shares W_gate's directions, rescaled per latent by e^(r_i).

A step has no gradient, so the L1 penalty goes on ReLU of the gate pre-activation, and an auxiliary term asks those same values to reconstruct x through a frozen (stop-gradient) copy of the decoder. Only gate parameters learn from these two terms, so the magnitudes are never shrunk.

blocks.title: The pentagon input through a Gated SAE

scenes.caption: Same input as lesson 2, x = (0.8, 0). W_gate rows are the five pentagon directions, b_gate = -0.309 (the old bias), r = 0 and b_mag = 0, b_dec = 0.
Gate pre-activations: dot products minus 0.309. Only latent 0 is positive (0.491), so only its gate opens. The neighbours' 0.247 leaks fall to -0.062.
Magnitude path: ReLU of the plain dot products with no bias, 0.8 for latent 0. The leaks show here (0.247) but their gates are shut.
Multiply: f = (0.8, 0, 0, 0, 0), so x-hat = (0.8, 0) with zero error and L0 = 1. Compare the plain ReLU SAE of lesson 2, which fired the same latent at a shrunk 0.491.
The shrinkage has not vanished; it moved. The L1 term sees ReLU(pi_gate) = 0.491, and the auxiliary reconstruction from it is (0.491, 0), error 0.095. That signal trains only the gate.

blocks.md:
With shared directions, a gated encoder is the same as one linear map followed by a jumping activation: a latent outputs 0 until its magnitude pre-activation passes the threshold $\theta_i = b_{mag,i} - e^{r_i} b_{gate,i}$, then passes the value through. In the pentagon that threshold is $0 - 1 \times (-0.309) = 0.309$.

**JumpReLU SAEs** (Rajamanoharan et al., 2024) make that activation the whole design: a normal elementwise encoder in which every latent $i$ has its own learned threshold $\theta_i$. Below the threshold the latent is 0; above it, the value passes through unchanged. Hence the name: a ReLU whose output jumps from 0 straight to $\theta_i$ at the threshold instead of rising smoothly from 0. Unlike TopK, the number of active latents can vary from token to token.

blocks.caption: H is the Heaviside step: 1 for a positive input, 0 otherwise, so z times H(z minus theta) keeps z only above theta. The penalty is a true L0 count: lambda times the number of active latents.

blocks.md: The step and the count both have zero gradient almost everywhere, so JumpReLU training uses **straight-through estimators**: the forward pass uses the real step, and the backward pass substitutes a stand-in derivative, a **pseudo-derivative** (written with the symbol $\eth$). For $\theta$ it is nonzero only when a pre-activation $z$ lands in a narrow window of width $\varepsilon$ (the kernel bandwidth) around the threshold. The paper uses a rectangle kernel $K$: 1 inside the window, 0 outside. Pre-activations far from $\theta$ say nothing about where $\theta$ should be; borderline ones do.

blocks.caption: Left: raising theta past a borderline z removes an output of size about theta. Middle: it also removes one count from L0. Chaining these with the loss gives each in-window token a theta gradient of (I minus lambda)/epsilon, where I = 2 theta d_i . (x - x-hat).

blocks.title: Which tokens move a JumpReLU threshold, and which way

scenes.caption: One latent, theta = 0.5, lambda = 0.1 and a wide bandwidth eps = 0.1 so the window [0.45, 0.55] is visible (real runs use 0.001). Three tokens: A, B and C.
C sits at 0.90, outside the window: it contributes nothing, however large its residual. A (just above theta) and B (just below) are both in the window.
Reconstruction part I/eps with I = 2 theta d.(x - x-hat): 2.5 for A, whose residual along d_i is large, and 0.3 for B.
Sparsity part: every in-window token adds -lambda/eps = -1.0, a push to raise theta and switch the latent off more often.
Totals: A gives +1.5 (gradient descent lowers theta, keep the latent on: it was needed), B gives -0.7 (raise theta). Batch mean (1.5 - 0.7 + 0)/3 = 0.267 > 0, so theta moves down.

blocks.title: ReLU, shifted ReLU and JumpReLU

scenes.caption: Plain ReLU passes the 0.247 interference leak through: too many latents fire.
A negative bias is ReLU(z - theta): leaks below theta are removed, but every surviving value is shifted down by theta. That is the shrinkage from lesson 2.
JumpReLU with theta = 0.4 zeroes the 0.247 leak yet passes 0.8 through unchanged, so the pentagon example reconstructs exactly with L0 = 1.
Each latent learns its own theta. A higher threshold means fewer firings; lambda on the L0 term controls how hard training pushes thresholds up.

blocks.md:
DeepMind reports that at a fixed L0 on Gemma 2 9B, JumpReLU SAEs reconstruct at least as well as TopK and better than Gated SAEs, while being cheaper to train than either: one forward and backward pass with an elementwise activation, no partial sort. JumpReLU is the architecture behind Gemma Scope. In the JumpReLU paper, $\varepsilon = 0.001$ (and an initial threshold of 0.001) worked well across models, layers and sites, assuming activations normalised to unit mean squared norm.

That assumption is a preprocessing step every real run needs: **activation normalisation**. Raw activation norms differ by orders of magnitude between layers and sites, which rescales the reconstruction loss and with it the right $\lambda$ and $\varepsilon$. Gemma Scope divides every activation by one fixed scalar so that $\mathbb{E}\|\mathbf{x}\|^2 = 1$, and after training folds that scalar back into the weights so users can feed raw activations. (Gao et al. instead subtract each vector's mean over its entries and scale it to unit norm.) Lesson 8 applies the scalar version to GPT-2.

L1 penalises size, so it shrinks every active latent. TopK (fixed k), Gated (separate gate) and JumpReLU (learned per-latent thresholds with an L0 penalty) all separate deciding which latents fire from estimating how big they are.
TopK fixes L0 = k on every token, even when a token needs more or fewer features. JumpReLU and L1 SAEs let L0 vary, so their reported L0 is an average over tokens.

blocks.question: You switch an SAE from L1 to TopK and keep everything else the same. Which hyperparameter replaces lambda as the main sparsity knob?
options: k, the number of latents kept per token
The learning rate
The number of latents M
The kernel bandwidth epsilon
blocks.explain: TopK sets sparsity directly: L0 equals k. There is no sparsity term in the loss, so there is no lambda to tune. Epsilon belongs to JumpReLU training.

blocks.question: An L1 SAE's latents look right on inspection, but its reconstructions are consistently a bit too short (smaller norm than x). What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: Dead latents; resample them
The learning rate is too high; lower it
Shrinkage from the L1 penalty; use TopK, JumpReLU or a Gated SAE, or re-fit magnitudes on the chosen latents
The dictionary is too large; reduce M
blocks.explain: L1 pulls every active magnitude down by about lambda/2 (in the one-latent case), so x-hat is systematically small. Architectures that decouple selection from magnitude remove this bias.

lessons.title: Training at scale: dead latents and feature splitting

blocks.md:
A **dead latent** never activates. It wastes a column of the dictionary and its compute. Scaling Monosemanticity and Gao et al. both call a latent dead if it has not fired over 10 million tokens (Towards Monosemanticity, whose A/1 numbers appear below, used 100 million examples).

Death happens because a latent whose pre-activation is negative on every input gets no gradient through the ReLU (or never makes the top k), so nothing pulls it back. It gets worse with width: more latents compete to explain the same data.

The numbers below use Towards Monosemanticity's naming. Its dictionaries are runs on a one-layer transformer called A: A/0 has 512 latents, A/1 has 4,096, A/2 has 16,384, and so on up to A/5 with 131,072. A single latent is written run then index, such as A/0/341.

blocks.title: Reported fraction of dead latents

scenes.caption: Towards Monosemanticity, run A/1: 168 of 4,096 latents dead (4.1%), with dead-latent resampling already on. Another 292 (7.1%) fired on under 1 in a million examples.
Scaling Monosemanticity on Claude 3 Sonnet: roughly 2%, 35% and 65% dead as the dictionary grows from 1M to 4M to 34M. The 34M SAE had about 12M live latents.

OpenAI saw up to 90% dead latents in ablation runs (training with the fixes switched off), but with their two fixes only 7% of the 16M-latent GPT-4 SAE was dead. Different models and recipes, so compare trends, not exact values.

blocks.md:
Three fixes appear in the papers:

1. **Resampling** (Towards Monosemanticity): every so often, re-seed dead latents on the inputs the SAE currently reconstructs worst (recipe below).
2. **Encoder initialised to the decoder's transpose** (Gao et al.): each latent starts out detecting the same direction it writes, so it begins life near data it can explain.
3. **AuxK auxiliary loss** (Gao et al., the name joining auxiliary and top-k; similar to 'ghost grads', an extra loss Anthropic used to give dead latents gradient): make the dead latents try to explain what the live ones missed.

Resampling, as Towards Monosemanticity ran it, at training steps 25,000, 50,000, 75,000 and 100,000:

1. Find the latents that have not fired in any of the previous 12,500 steps.
2. Compute the SAE's loss on a random subset of 819,200 inputs.
3. Give each input a probability of being picked proportional to the **square** of its loss.
4. For each dead latent, sample one input this way, scale it to unit length and make it that latent's decoder column.
5. Set the latent's encoder row to the same input, rescaled to 0.2 times the average encoder-row norm of the live latents, and set its encoder bias to 0.
6. Reset the Adam optimiser state for every modified weight and bias.

The small encoder norm makes the reborn latent fire only weakly, and only on inputs like its seed, so it disturbs the rest of the dictionary little. The authors note it still causes loss spikes, and resampling too often makes training diverge.

In AuxK, the residual error is $\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{x} - \hat{\mathbf{x}}$, what the main reconstruction missed; this 'residual' has nothing to do with the residual stream. Gao et al. typically use $k_{aux} = 512$, a power of two close to half of `d_model` (512 for GPT-2 small), and $\alpha = 1/32$.

blocks.caption: e is the residual error. e-hat is the dead latents' reconstruction of it from z_dead, the top k_aux pre-activations among latents flagged dead. Total loss: the usual squared error plus alpha times the squared gap between e and e-hat. Dead latents now receive gradient from the residual error.

blocks.title: One TopK training step with AuxK
blocks.code:
z_pre = W_enc @ (x - b_pre)            # [M]
z = topk(z_pre, k)                      # main latents
x_hat = W_dec @ z + b_pre
loss = sum((x - x_hat) ** 2)

steps_since_fired[z > 0] = 0
steps_since_fired[z == 0] += tokens_per_step
dead = steps_since_fired > 10_000_000

if dead.any():
    e = x - x_hat                       # what the live latents missed
    z_dead = topk(where(dead, z_pre, -inf), k_aux)
    e_hat = W_dec @ z_dead
    loss += alpha * sum((e - e_hat) ** 2)

loss.backward(); adam.step()
normalize_columns(W_dec)               # unit-norm decoder

scenes.caption: Normal TopK forward pass: encode, keep k, decode, squared error. Only the k chosen latents receive gradient.
Track how long each latent has been silent. Latents silent for 10 million tokens are flagged dead.
AuxK: take the residual error and reconstruct it using only the top k_aux dead latents. Their best guesses now get gradient.
Update, then keep decoder columns unit norm (one of several conventions). Gao et al. report AuxK adds only about 10% compute because the encoder pass is shared.

blocks.md:
**Feature splitting** is the second scale effect. Train SAEs of different widths on the same activations and compare. Towards Monosemanticity found that features come in families: going from 512 latents (A/0) to 4,096 (A/1) to 16,384 (A/2), the number of latents specific to base64 text went from 1 to 3 to many more.

A coarse latent that fires on 'the' in mathematical prose (A/0/341) predicts generic maths tokens such as 'the theorem'. Wider runs contain more specific relatives: a machine-learning version (A/2/15021) predicting 'the dataset', an abstract algebra and topology version (A/2/4878) predicting 'the quotient', and a gravitation and field theory version (A/2/2609) predicting 'the Lagrangian'.

blocks.title: Feature splitting as the dictionary grows

scenes.caption: A 512-latent dictionary has one broad latent for 'the' in technical maths writing. Its top predicted next tokens are generic: the denominator, the remainder, the theorem.
The 16,384-latent run has specific relatives with specific predictions (the classifier; the subgroup; the spacetime). Simplified: the paper finds splits and merges, not a clean tree.
Counts for base64 contexts across widths: 1, then 3, then many. More capacity buys finer distinctions of the same territory.

blocks.prompt: If wider SAEs keep splitting features into finer ones, what is the 'correct' number of latents for an SAE on a given layer?
blocks.reveal: There probably is not one. Towards Monosemanticity conjectures an idealised set of very many fine features, of which any finite dictionary returns a coarser covering. Width is then a resolution knob: small SAEs give a summary, large ones give detail. Gemma Scope releases a ladder of widths on the same site (2^14 to 2^19 latents on some layers) precisely so researchers can study this.

blocks.md:
Which activations to train on is a choice too. Gemma Scope trained SAEs at three **sites** in every layer: the attention output (the concatenated head outputs before the output projection $W_O$, following Kissane et al.), the MLP output, and the residual stream after the MLP.

- **Residual stream**: the most used, because one SAE sees everything earlier layers wrote. Gemma Scope finds its delta LM loss consistently higher than for MLP or attention SAEs at similar FVU: an error here reaches every later layer, while an error in one sublayer's output is small relative to the whole residual stream.
- **MLP output**: the site Towards Monosemanticity used; lower delta loss than the residual stream at similar FVU.
- **Attention output**: Kissane et al. found interpretable families here, such as long-range context, short-range context and induction features, and estimated that at least 90% of GPT-2 small's attention heads are polysemantic.

A close relative, the **transcoder**, is trained to predict an MLP's output from its input instead of reconstructing one activation. It is the building block of the next course, Circuit tracing and attribution graphs, so it is not covered here.

Dead latents grow with width; fix them with resampling, encoder-equals-decoder-transpose init and an AuxK loss. Feature splitting means the dictionary you get depends on width, so a feature is always 'a feature at this resolution'.
A latent dying is not the same as a feature being absent from the model. It only means this SAE found no use for that column, often because of optimisation, not because the concept is missing.

blocks.question: Your 4M-latent SAE has 40% dead latents. Which change directly gives those latents a training signal?
options: Increase lambda so the remaining latents are sparser
Decrease the batch size
Remove the decoder bias
Add an auxiliary loss that reconstructs the main SAE's residual error using only the dead latents' top activations
blocks.explain: A dead latent gets no gradient from the main loss because it never fires. AuxK forces the top k_aux dead latents to predict the residual error, giving them gradient toward directions the live latents miss. Increasing lambda would push even more latents off.

blocks.question: You compare a 4,096-latent and a 65,536-latent SAE on the same layer. The smaller one has a 'Python code' latent; the larger has several latents for different Python contexts and none that matches it exactly. What does this indicate?
options: The larger SAE is broken
Feature splitting: the wider dictionary covers the same concept at finer resolution
The smaller SAE has dead latents
Python is not represented in the model
blocks.explain: This is the expected pattern from Towards Monosemanticity: wider dictionaries refine broad latents into families of more specific ones.

blocks.question: A residual-stream SAE and an MLP-output SAE in the same layer have the same FVU. Which do you expect to raise the language model's loss more when spliced in, and why?
options: The MLP SAE, because MLP outputs are sparser
Neither: equal FVU means equal downstream loss
The residual-stream SAE, because its error is carried into every later layer, while an MLP error is small next to the whole residual stream
The residual-stream SAE, because residual SAEs have more dead latents
blocks.explain: Gemma Scope reports consistently higher delta loss for residual-stream SAEs at similar FVU. FVU measures error relative to that site's own variance; what matters downstream is how big the error is relative to everything later layers read.

lessons.title: Reading a latent: activating examples, logit effects, autointerp

blocks.md:
You have a trained SAE with 24,576 latents. Latent 5,395 fires on about 0.03% of tokens according to the SAE's released sparsity file (0.05% in our own 3,000-document sample), and on the prompt 'The Golden Gate Bridge is in San Francisco' it fires at 38.3 on ' Bridge' and nowhere else in the sentence. What does it mean, and how sure can you be?

Everything in this lesson that mentions latent 5,395 is real: it comes from the released GPT-2 small SAE at the residual stream entering block 6 (Joseph Bloom's `gpt2-small-res-jb`, which lesson 8 loads), run over 3,000 Pile documents. Neuronpedia's automatic labels for it read 'references to physical structures like bridges' and 'instances of the word bridge'.

The standard view of one latent is a **feature dashboard**, as on Neuronpedia (an open site hosting dashboards for Gemma Scope and many other released SAEs). It has three parts, each answering a different question:

1. **Activating examples**: on which tokens, in which contexts, does the latent fire, and how strongly?
2. **Activation density**: how often does it fire at all?
3. **Logit effect**: if the latent's decoder direction is added to the residual stream, which next tokens become more or less likely?

The first two describe what the latent **reads**; the third describes what it **writes**. A trustworthy name has to agree with both.

Do not stop at the top examples. Towards Monosemanticity found that many polysemantic neurons look monosemantic if you only read their maximal examples and are revealed as polysemantic lower down the activation range. So its authors split the range from 0 to the maximum activation into 11 evenly spaced **activation intervals** and sampled examples from each. Paulo et al. (2024) did the same with deciles and found that explanations written from top examples only are more specific but miss the weaker activations, while explanations from samples across the range hold up better on weaker activations, though they can come out too broad.

blocks.title: Latent 5,395: firings per activation interval

scenes.caption: 364,443 tokens, 194 firings, maximum 46.1. Split the range into five equal intervals: 169 of the 194 firings sit in the lowest one.
Top interval (36.9 to 46.1): 'may include bridges', 'the Golden Gate Bridge', 'right next to the new bridge'. The top 8 examples are all the word bridge. Reading only these, the label is obvious.
Middle intervals: 'Cambrid' (of Cambridge), 'Woodbridge', 'London Bridge', 'PCI bridge'. Still bridge-like, now including word pieces inside place names.
Lowest interval, where most firings live: ' coronary' in 'percutaneous coronary', 'roadway', 'AN' in 'SWAN'. Weak firings on unrelated tokens: the polysemantic tail that top examples hide.

blocks.md: **Activation density** is the fraction of tokens on which a latent is nonzero. Plotted on a log10 scale across all latents, it is one of the quickest health checks. Towards Monosemanticity found these histograms often bimodal: an **ultralow-density** cluster (around $10^{-7}$ in one run) whose latents were almost never interpretable, and a higher-density cluster whose latents almost always were. Dead latents sit at minus infinity, off the chart. At the other end, SAEBench lists uninterpretable high-frequency latents as a problem that reconstruction metrics miss.

blocks.title: Activation density of all 24,576 latents (released file)

scenes.caption: Counts of latents by firing frequency, from the sparsity file shipped with this SAE. Most latents fire on between 1 in 10,000 and 1 in 100 tokens; 12 never fired.
Latent 5,395 has log10 density -3.57 (about 1 in 3,700 tokens), in the 1e-4 to 1e-3 bin with most latents. The 1,012 latents firing on more than 1% of tokens deserve extra scrutiny.

blocks.md:
The **logit effect** asks what a latent writes. Its decoder column $\mathbf{d}_i$ is a direction in the residual stream. Pass it through the final normalisation's gain and the unembedding matrix $W_U$ (which turns the last residual vector into one logit per vocabulary token) and you get one number per token: how much adding $\mathbf{d}_i$ raises or lowers that token's logit. Softmax ignores a constant shift, so only differences matter; Towards Monosemanticity shifts each latent's values so the median is zero.

This is a linear shortcut. It ignores every layer between the SAE and the output, so for a middle-layer latent it shows only the direct path. Treat it as a hypothesis generator and cross-check with activations.

blocks.caption: Logit effect of latent i: the unembedding applied to the decoder direction (scaled by the final norm's gain gamma, with its centring folded in), shifted so the median token gets zero. Large positive entries are tokens the latent promotes.

blocks.title: Toy logit effects: a 'say Paris' latent and a diffuse one

scenes.caption: A made-up 4-dimensional model (norm gain 1) with a 6-token vocabulary. Latent 1's unit decoder column is (0.8, 0.4, -0.4, -0.2). After the median shift it promotes Paris (0.99) and France (0.93) and suppresses bridge (0.43 below the median, shown as size).

Latent 2, decoder about (0.30, 0.30, 0.30, 0.85): the largest effect is only 0.29 (the), then 0.21 (of), with bridge at -0.25. No token stands out: a diffuse latent whose name cannot come from its logits.

Read together with activations: if latent 1 fires on 'The Eiffel Tower is in' and promotes Paris, both views agree on 'about to say Paris'. If they disagree, the name is suspect. Bar height is size; colour shows sign (red: suppressed).

blocks.md:
Reading dashboards by hand does not scale to millions of latents, so the names on Neuronpedia are written by language models. The template is Bills et al. (OpenAI, 2023), built to explain GPT-2 neurons with GPT-4:

1. **Explain.** Show an explainer model five top-activating 64-token excerpts, with each token's activation rescaled to an integer from 0 to 10 (the latent's maximum maps to 10), and ask for a one-sentence explanation.
2. **Simulate.** Give a simulator model only the explanation and new text, and have it predict a 0 to 10 activation for every token (the expected value of its probabilities over the digits).
3. **Score.** The explanation's score is the **correlation** between simulated and true activations: 1 means the explanation predicts the latent perfectly, about 0 means it is unrelated.

Over all of GPT-2 XL's MLP neurons they found more than 1,000 whose explanations scored at least 0.8. Towards Monosemanticity ran the same loop with Claude and found its SAE features far easier to explain than neurons.

blocks.title: Simulation scoring on ten tokens

scenes.caption: True activations of a latent (rescaled to 0 to 10) on ten tokens. It fires on Paris and France and nowhere else.
Explanation A, 'names of French places': the simulator predicts 9 on Paris, 7 on France and 1 on Eiffel and Tower. Correlation with the truth: 0.99.
Explanation B, 'famous landmarks': 6 and 7 on Eiffel Tower, 4 on Paris, 0 on France. Correlation 0.13: the explanation fits the topic of the text but not the tokens the latent fires on.

blocks.md:
Simulation needs a judgment on every token, which is expensive. Paulo et al. (EleutherAI, 2024) built an open pipeline, the `delphi` library, that explains SAE latents with Llama 3.1 70B from 40 examples of 32 tokens and scores them in cheaper ways:

- **Detection**: show the scorer whole contexts, some activating and some not, and ask which ones the explanation says should activate. Accuracy over both kinds measures precision and recall.
- **Fuzzing**: mark candidate tokens inside each context and ask whether the marks sit on the right tokens. This correlates best with simulation (Spearman about 0.7 in their comparison).
- **Intervention scoring**: steer with the latent and ask whether the explanation predicts the change in the model's text. It rescues latents better described by what they cause than by where they fire.

Detection and fuzzing cost at least 5 times less than simulation run all at once, and about 30 times less than simulation token by token.

blocks.prompt: A detection run uses 5 activating and 5 non-activating contexts. The scorer, given the explanation, says 'activates' for 4 of the activating contexts and for 1 of the non-activating ones. What is the detection accuracy, and what does the false positive tell you?
blocks.reveal: Correct calls: 4 activating contexts plus 4 of the 5 non-activating ones, so 8 of 10, an accuracy of 0.8. The miss is a recall failure (the explanation is too narrow for one context that does activate), and the false positive is a precision failure (the explanation is too broad, covering a context where the latent stays silent). Bills et al. found explainers often ignore such negative evidence: a neuron firing on 'not all' was explained as 'the term all', which only text containing 'all' without 'not' exposes.

blocks.code:
import torch
from sae_lens import SAE
sae = SAE.from_pretrained(release="gpt2-small-res-jb",
                          sae_id="blocks.6.hook_resid_pre", device="cpu")
LATENT = 5395

def resid6(ids):                       # GPT-2 residual entering block 6
    h = model(ids, output_hidden_states=True).hidden_states[6]
    return h - h.mean(-1, keepdim=True)  # this SAE expects centred vectors

acts, ctxs = [], []
with torch.no_grad():
    for text in texts[:3000]:
        ids = torch.tensor([[tok.bos_token_id] + tok(text)["input_ids"][:127]])
        a = sae.encode(resid6(ids))[0, :, LATENT]
        for p in range(1, ids.shape[1]):          # skip BOS
            acts.append(a[p].item())
            ctxs.append(tok.decode(ids[0, max(1, p - 8):p + 1]))

acts = torch.tensor(acts)
print("density", (acts > 0).float().mean().item())
edges = torch.linspace(0, acts.max(), 6)          # 5 activation intervals
for lo, hi in zip(edges[:-1], edges[1:]):
    idx = ((acts > lo) & (acts <= hi)).nonzero().flatten()
    print(f"({lo:.1f}, {hi:.1f}]", len(idx), [ctxs[i] for i in idx[:3]])
for i in acts.topk(8).indices:
    print(round(acts[i].item(), 2), ctxs[i])
blocks.caption: SAELens (lesson 8) downloads the SAE; model, tok: GPT-2 small from transformers; texts: Pile documents. Real output: density 0.00053, intervals 169 / 6 / 1 / 3 / 15, top 46.1 on 'formed by a bridge'. The SAE was trained on zero-mean residual vectors, hence the centring (lesson 8 explains).

blocks.md:
Pitfalls to keep in mind whenever you read a name:

- **Top-only explanations are too narrow or too broad.** Lower activation intervals were less consistent with the explanation in Towards Monosemanticity's manual study, and most of a latent's activations live there.
- **Correlation is not function.** Every score above checks whether an explanation predicts where the latent fires. None checks that the model uses the latent for what the name says. Bills et al. found that even explanations scoring 0.9 by correlation lost much more when the simulated activations replaced the real ones inside the network.
- **The illusion of a clean story.** A latent can look like 'starts with S' on every example you read and still miss a whole subset of S-words (lesson 7 shows why).

So treat a name as a hypothesis and test it causally: clamp the latent as in lesson 6 and see whether the model's behaviour changes the way the name predicts.

A latent's name comes from what it reads (activating examples across the whole activation range, plus its density) and what it writes (its logit effect). Automated pipelines write names with one LLM and score them with another by simulation, detection or fuzzing; all of these are correlational, so finish with a causal check.

A Neuronpedia label is an LLM's guess from a sample of examples, not ground truth. Before you build on a latent, read examples from its lower activation intervals and a few non-activating contexts that seem to match the name.

blocks.question: An explanation scores 0.95 on simulation using only top-activating excerpts, but 0.30 when the excerpts are sampled across the whole activation range. What is the best reading?
options: The explanation fits the strongest activations but not the weaker ones that make up most firings; it is too narrow
The latent is dead
The simulator model is broken; trust the 0.95
The latent must be monosemantic because 0.95 is high
blocks.explain: Top examples can make a latent look cleaner than it is. Towards Monosemanticity and Paulo et al. sample across activation intervals precisely because weaker activations often follow a broader or different pattern.

blocks.question: Which check would most directly test the name 'promotes the token Paris' for a residual-stream latent?
options: Count how often the latent fires
Clamp the latent higher on prompts where it is off and measure whether the probability of ' Paris' rises
Raise its autointerp detection score
Look at its top five activating examples again
blocks.explain: The name is a claim about what the latent writes. An intervention measures that causally; activation-based scores and density only describe where it fires. The logit effect suggests it, and the clamp confirms it through the real network.

lessons.title: Measuring an SAE and steering a model with its features

blocks.md:
Three numbers summarise an SAE (definitions as in Gemma Scope and Gao et al.):

- **L0**: the average number of active latents per token, $\mathbb{E}\,\|\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x})\|_0$. Lower is sparser and usually easier to interpret.
- **Fraction of variance unexplained (FVU)**, which OpenAI calls normalised MSE: reconstruction MSE divided by the MSE of always predicting the mean activation. The denominator is the activations' variance, their mean squared distance from their mean, so FVU is the share of that variance the SAE leaves unexplained: 0 is perfect, 1 is no better than always guessing the mean. **Fraction of variance explained** is $1 - \text{FVU}$.
- **Downstream loss**: splice $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ into the model in place of $\mathbf{x}$, keep running the forward pass, and measure next-token cross-entropy. **Delta LM loss** is the increase over the clean model. **Loss recovered** compares the cross-entropy (CE) of three runs: clean, with the SAE spliced in, and with the activation **zero-ablated** (replaced by zeros).

blocks.caption: FVU: mean squared reconstruction error over the mean squared distance of x from its mean x-bar. Loss recovered: (CE zero minus CE SAE) over (CE zero minus CE clean), the share of the damage from zeroing that the SAE undoes. 100% means the SAE is as good as the real activation.

blocks.title: Computing L0 and FVU on a 4-token batch (pentagon TopK SAE)

scenes.caption: Four activations: t0 = 0.8 d0, t1 = 0.8 d0 + 0.6 d1, t2 = 0.5 d3, t3 = 0. Their mean is (0.345, 0.069); the baseline MSE of predicting it is 0.423.
TopK with k = 1. L0 per token 1, 1, 1, 0 (the zero token activates nothing), mean L0 = 0.75. Only t1 has error (0.326): it has two features. MSE 0.081, FVU 0.193, so 80.7% of variance explained.
k = 2. Mean L0 = 1.5. t1 improves to 0.124 but t0 and t2 now admit interference latents. MSE 0.052, FVU 0.123 (87.7% explained). Doubling L0 bought 7 points of variance.

blocks.md:
Published numbers for scale: Scaling Monosemanticity's three Sonnet SAEs had fewer than 300 active latents per token on average and explained at least 65% of the variance. Towards Monosemanticity's A/1 recovered 79% of the loss reduction the MLP layer provides; its 131,072-latent run A/5 recovered 94.5%.

Gao et al. warn that loss recovered flatters SAEs on the residual stream: zero-ablating the whole residual stream is catastrophic, so even poor SAEs score high. Their 16M GPT-4 SAE scored 98.2% on that metric, yet substituting it into GPT-4 gave a loss matching a model trained with about 10% of GPT-4's pretraining compute.

blocks.prompt: Illustrative numbers: the clean model's loss is 3.00 nats (cross-entropy measured with natural logs), with your SAE spliced in it is 3.20, and with the residual stream zeroed it is 10.0. What is the loss recovered, and is this SAE good?
blocks.reveal: $(10.0 - 3.20)/(10.0 - 3.00) = 97.1\%$, which sounds excellent. But delta LM loss is 0.20 nats, a large degradation for a language model. Gemma Scope uses delta LM loss as its primary fidelity metric, and notes residual-stream SAEs show higher delta loss than MLP or attention SAEs even at similar FVU, since small residual errors propagate through every later layer.

blocks.md:
Zero is an arbitrary baseline. **Mean ablation** replaces the activation with its average over the dataset instead, which removes everything token-specific but keeps the constant part later layers always expect. Loss recovered then uses $\text{CE}_{mean}$ in place of $\text{CE}_{zero}$. Mean ablation hurts less, so the same SAE scores lower.

Illustrative: if mean-ablating gives 7.5 nats in the example above, loss recovered is $(7.5 - 3.20)/(7.5 - 3.00) = 95.6\%$ instead of 97.1%. For a single MLP layer whose mean ablation costs only 0.4 nats (3.40), the same 0.20 nats of damage scores $(3.40 - 3.20)/(3.40 - 3.00) = 50\%$.

Measured in lesson 8 on GPT-2 small (residual stream entering block 6, our TopK SAE with $k = 32$): clean 3.51, SAE 3.71, zero-ablated 13.22, mean-ablated 8.39 nats.

blocks.title: Loss recovered depends on the ablation baseline

scenes.caption: Illustrative residual-stream SAE (clean 3.00, SAE 3.20): 97.1% with a zero-ablation baseline (10.0 nats), 95.6% with a mean-ablation baseline (7.5).
A sublayer whose mean ablation costs only 0.4 nats: the same 0.20-nat damage now recovers just 50%. The baseline, not the SAE, changed.
Real GPT-2 run from lesson 8: 97.9% against zero ablation, 95.8% against mean ablation, for a delta LM loss of 0.21 nats.

blocks.md:
These metrics trade off: lower L0 or fewer latents means higher error. Gao et al. fit a **scaling law**, a formula fitted to many training runs that predicts the error from size, for TopK SAEs on GPT-4 at convergence (trained until the error stops improving), in the number of latents $n$ and sparsity $k$ (natural logs; it holds only for small $k$). In words, the normalised MSE is e raised to the power alpha plus beta k times ln k plus beta n times ln n plus gamma times ln k times ln n, plus a second term, e raised to the power zeta plus eta times ln k:

$L(n,k) = e^{\alpha + \beta_k \ln k + \beta_n \ln n + \gamma \ln k \ln n} + e^{\zeta + \eta \ln k}$

with $\alpha = -0.50$, $\beta_k = 0.26$, $\beta_n = -0.017$, $\gamma = -0.042$, $\zeta = -1.32$, $\eta = -0.085$. The second term is an irreducible floor that falls only as $k$ grows.

blocks.title: Normalised MSE vs number of latents (Gao et al. GPT-4 fit)

scenes.caption: k = 32: FVU falls from 0.533 at 10K latents to 0.299 at 16M (about 2^24). Each 10x more latents helps less.
k = 512: 0.392 at 10K and 0.187 at 16M. More active latents lowers both the curve and the floor, at the cost of a denser, harder-to-read code.
k = 16: 0.576 at 10K, 0.347 at 16M. The negative gamma makes the curve flatter for small k: very sparse codes gain less from extra width.

blocks.md: L0, FVU and downstream loss measure how faithfully an SAE compresses activations, not whether its latents are useful or correctly named. Benchmarks such as SAEBench add task-based metrics: **sparse probing** (can one to five latents classify a labelled concept?), an **absorption rate** (lesson 7) and an **automated interpretability score** (lesson 5). Lesson 7 shows that SAEs which win on the proxy metrics do not always win on these.

**Steering** tests whether a latent is causal, not just correlated. Scaling Monosemanticity's recipe: split the residual activation into the SAE reconstruction and the error, $\mathbf{x} = \text{SAE}(\mathbf{x}) + \text{error}(\mathbf{x})$. Replace SAE(x) with a version in which latent $i$ is clamped to a chosen value $c$, keep the error term unchanged, and run the downstream layers on the result, at every token position.

Because the decoder is linear, clamping is the same as adding a scaled copy of the latent's direction. The reconstruction is $\mathbf{b}_{dec} + \sum_j f_j \mathbf{d}_j$, so changing $f_i$ to $c$ moves it by exactly $(c - f_i)\,\mathbf{d}_i$, and reconstruction plus the unchanged error is $\mathbf{x}$ again:

blocks.caption: In words: the new activation x-prime is the edited reconstruction plus the old error, which equals x plus (c minus f_i) times d_i. Keeping the error term means everything the SAE fails to explain is left untouched; only the chosen feature changes.

blocks.title: Clamping latent 3 to 2.0 in the pentagon SAE

scenes.caption: Token t1 from before with k = 2: latents 0 and 1 active, reconstruction (1.247, 0.806), error (-0.262, -0.235).
Clamp latent 3 from 0 to 2.0. The new reconstruction is (-0.371, -0.370).
Add back the unchanged error: x' = (-0.633, -0.605), exactly x + 2.0 d3. This vector replaces x in all later layers.

blocks.md:
In Claude 3 Sonnet, clamping a Golden Gate Bridge latent to 10 times its maximum observed activation made the model describe itself as the bridge; clamping a transit-infrastructure latent to 5 times its maximum made it mention a bridge where it otherwise would not. Clamping a code-error latent produced hallucinated error messages on bug-free code. The authors also built few-shot steering vectors from mean activation differences (a direction computed as the average activation on a few prompts showing a concept minus the average on prompts without it) and found them generally less interpretable and less effective than feature steering in their case studies.

Other uses: Cunningham et al. patched SAE features to localise model behaviour on the indirect object identification task (completing 'When Mary and John went to the store, John gave a drink to' with 'Mary') more precisely than with PCA directions, and Gemma Scope releases SAEs on every layer for circuit-style analysis (tracing which components pass information to which to produce a behaviour).

Judge an SAE by sparsity (L0), reconstruction (FVU) and downstream loss together, then verify interpretations causally. Steering by clamping a latent equals adding $(c - f_i)$ times its decoder direction while keeping the SAE error.

High variance explained is not full understanding. Sonnet's SAEs explained at least 65% of variance, so a sizeable part of the activation lives in the error term, and a latent's top activating examples do not prove what it does. Use ablation or steering to check.

blocks.question: Two SAEs on the same residual-stream layer: A has L0 = 40 and FVU = 0.30; B has L0 = 400 and FVU = 0.10. Which conclusion is justified from these numbers alone?
options: Neither dominates; compare them on the same L0 or the same FVU, and check delta LM loss
B is strictly better because its FVU is lower
A is strictly better because it is sparser
They must have the same downstream loss because they share a layer
blocks.explain: SAEs live on a sparsity versus fidelity frontier. B buys lower error with ten times more active latents. Fair comparisons hold one axis fixed, and downstream loss can rank SAEs differently from MSE.

blocks.question: Why does the Scaling Monosemanticity steering recipe keep the SAE error term instead of feeding the edited reconstruction alone into later layers?
options: To make the latent's activation non-negative
Because the error term is always zero for TopK SAEs
So the only change to the activation is the chosen feature; dropping the error would also remove everything the SAE fails to reconstruct
To reduce memory use
blocks.explain: Replacing x with the reconstruction alone would apply two edits at once: the feature clamp and the loss of all unexplained structure. Keeping the error makes x' = x + (c - f_i) d_i.

blocks.question: You clamp a latent to a large negative value although the encoder never outputs negatives. What happens to the activation?
options: Nothing; negative clamps are clipped to zero
A negative multiple of the latent's decoder direction is added to x
The latent's decoder direction is deleted
All other latents are set to zero
blocks.explain: Scaling Monosemanticity notes that clamping to a negative value simply gives a negative multiple of the feature vector. In their code-error example, negative clamping made the model predict the output the code would have produced without the bug.

lessons.title: Where SAEs fall short: absorption, missing features and weak baselines

blocks.md:
Picture a latent that fires on tokens starting with the letter S: ' snake', ' sun', ' simple'. Its top examples look perfect, and its autointerp score from lesson 5 is high. Then you feed it ' short' and it stays silent, although the model clearly knows ' short' starts with S. A different latent, one that fires on ' short' and its variants, fired instead.

This is not a made-up story. Chanin et al. found exactly this in Gemma Scope: a layer 3 SAE (16k latents, L0 about 59) has latent 6510, which acts like a 'starts with S' classifier with an F1 of 0.81 (F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall), yet fails on ' short', where a token-specific 'short' latent, 1085, fires instead. This lesson covers why that happens, what else is known to go wrong with SAEs, and when a simpler tool is the better choice.

Two features form a **hierarchy** when one implies the other: every time the child ('this token is short') is present, the parent ('starts with S') is present too. An ideal dictionary would fire two latents on ' short': the parent and the child.

**Feature absorption** is what a sparsity objective prefers instead. The child latent's decoder direction swallows the parent's direction, so one latent reconstructs both, and the parent latent learns to switch off whenever the child is present. Reconstruction is still perfect, but one fewer latent fires. The parent latent now has a hole: it looks monosemantic on its top examples but silently misses an arbitrary-looking subset of the tokens it should cover. Chanin et al. call such latents gerrymandered.

blocks.title: Absorption on a parent and child feature

scenes.caption: The hierarchy: C (the word short) never appears without P (starts with S). The ideal dictionary has one latent per feature.
Ideal solution on ' short': both latents fire, each at 1.0. Reconstruction is exact and L0 on this token is 2.
Absorbed solution: latent 1's decoder becomes P + C (scaled to unit length) and latent 0 learns to stay off when C is present. Reconstruction is still exact, with L0 = 1.
Result: latent 0 reads as 'starts with S' on its top examples but has a hole at ' short'. Anyone using it as an S detector gets false negatives.

blocks.md:
Run the numbers on a toy in the style of Chanin et al.'s: three orthogonal unit features. Parent P fires on 25% of tokens. Child C fires on 20% of the tokens that have P (so on 5% of all tokens), never without P. An unrelated feature F fires on 5%. Both dictionaries below reconstruct every token exactly, so only the sparsity term differs.

- Expected L0: ideal $0.25 + 0.05 + 0.05 = 0.35$; absorbed $0.20 + 0.05 + 0.05 = 0.30$, since P-and-C tokens now use one latent.
- Expected L1 with decoder norms (lesson 2's penalty): on a child token the ideal pays $1 + 1 = 2$, while the absorbed latent with unit decoder $(P + C)/\sqrt{2}$ fires at $\sqrt{2} \approx 1.414$. Averaged: 0.35 against 0.321.

Either penalty prefers absorption, and the parent latent's recall (the share of true P tokens it fires on) drops from 100% to 80%.

blocks.title: Toy hierarchy: the sparsity term prefers the absorbed dictionary

scenes.caption: Expected active latents per token: 0.35 for the ideal dictionary, 0.30 for the absorbed one. Same reconstruction error (zero), so an L0 penalty or TopK prefers absorption.
Expected L1 with decoder norms: 0.35 against 0.321. The L1 penalty prefers absorption too, because one latent at 1.414 is cheaper than two at 1.0.

Matryoshka check: reconstruct with latent 0 alone. Ideal leaves only C (error 1) on child tokens, absorbed leaves P + C (error 2): expected error 0.10 against 0.15, so the nested loss now favours the ideal dictionary.

blocks.md:
Absorption does not go away with the knobs you already have. Chanin et al. measured an absorption rate on a first-letter task across hundreds of Gemma Scope SAEs (and their own SAEs on Qwen2 0.5B and Llama 3.2 1B) and found that wider and sparser SAEs absorb **more**: both push towards fewer, more specific latents. Their conclusion is that varying SAE size or sparsity is insufficient to fix it.

Notice how this differs from feature splitting in lesson 4. Splitting replaces a broad latent with a family of narrower ones that together cover the territory. Absorption leaves the broad latent in place but punches holes in it, which is worse for anyone who reads the broad latent as a detector.

**Matryoshka SAEs** (Bussmann et al. 2025, named after Russian nesting dolls) attack the cause. Order the $m$ latents and pick nested sizes $m_1 < m_2 < \dots < m_n = m$. Each prefix, the first $m_i$ latents alone, must reconstruct the input as well as it can, and the losses are summed. Early latents are used by every prefix, so they are pushed to be general; later latents only help the larger prefixes, so they can specialise without stealing the general direction.

In the toy above, the size-1 prefix makes the difference: the absorbed dictionary leaves P + C unexplained on child tokens and pays 0.15 instead of 0.10. On Gemma-2-2B the authors use 65,536 latents with prefixes 2,048, 6,144, 14,336, 30,720 and 65,536. The cost is a little reconstruction: at L0 = 40 the Matryoshka SAE explains 70% of the variance against 72% for a plain BatchTopK SAE.

blocks.caption: Matryoshka loss: for every prefix size m in the set M, reconstruct x using only the first m latents and their decoder columns, and add up the squared errors. L_aux is the AuxK loss from lesson 4.

blocks.md: **BatchTopK** (Bussmann et al. 2024), which the Matryoshka SAEs above use, relaxes TopK from one token to a batch. For a batch of $B$ tokens it keeps the $B \times k$ largest pre-activations anywhere in the batch, so the average L0 is still $k$ but an information-poor token can use one latent while a dense one uses 80. The authors observe exactly that: some tokens, notably the BOS token, activate only a single latent. Because a token's code now depends on its batch mates, inference replaces the batch rule with one global threshold $\theta$, estimated as the average of the smallest positive kept activation over many batches, which makes it a JumpReLU at test time. On GPT-2 small (layer 8) and Gemma 2 2B (layer 12) residual streams, BatchTopK reconstructs better than TopK at the same L0.

**SAE latents are not canonical units.** Leask et al. (2025) test the hope that SAEs find one fixed, complete list of atomic features. *SAE stitching* swaps latents between SAEs of different widths. Some latents of the larger SAE are *reconstruction latents*, finer versions that can replace a small SAE's latent; others are *novel latents* that improve the small SAE when added, so the small SAE was incomplete. *Meta-SAEs*, SAEs trained on another SAE's decoder columns, show the large SAE's latents are not atomic either: a latent for 'Einstein' decomposes into meta-latents such as 'scientist', 'Germany' and 'famous person'. The authors' advice is pragmatic: pick the dictionary size that suits your task instead of searching for the true one.

**Do SAEs beat simple baselines?** Kantamneni et al. (2025) trained probes on Gemma Scope SAE latents of Gemma-2-9B for 113 binary classification datasets, in four hard regimes: scarce data, class imbalance, label noise and covariate shift (test text that differs from training text, such as a translation). Adding SAE probes to a practitioner's toolbox of standard probes on the raw activations (logistic regression, PCA, k-nearest neighbours, XGBoost, small MLPs) gave no consistent advantage in any regime, and SAE probes generalised worse under covariate shift: one 'living room' latent scored 0.99 AUC (area under the ROC curve: 1 is perfect, 0.5 is chance) in distribution but 0.64 on French text, where it barely fires.

**AxBench** (Wu et al. 2025) compared methods on Gemma 2 models for detecting and steering 500 concepts. **Difference-in-means**, the mean activation on concept examples minus the mean on other examples, beat SAE latents on both tasks, and prompting beat every representation method at steering.

blocks.title: AxBench: SAE latents against simple supervised baselines

scenes.caption: Concept detection, mean AUROC over concepts and four model/layer settings. DiffMean 0.942 and a linear probe 0.940 lead; SAE latents chosen by their Neuronpedia label score 0.695.
Even picking the best SAE latent per concept with labelled data (0.917) trails the two supervised directions. AUROC: the chance a positive example outscores a negative one, 0.5 is random.
Steering, mean overall score (harmonic mean of concept, instruction and fluency ratings from an LLM judge). Prompting 0.894, DiffMean 0.239, SAE 0.165, SAE with AUROC pick 0.157.

blocks.md:
**SAEBench** (Karvonen et al. 2025) is a response to grading SAEs only by L0 and FVU. It runs eight metrics in four groups: *concept detection* (k-sparse probing, feature absorption), *interpretability* (automated interpretation, scored by an LLM judge as in lesson 5), *reconstruction* (loss recovered), and *feature disentanglement* (unlearning, spurious correlation removal, targeted probe perturbation, plus RAVEL, which checks that editing one attribute of an entity leaves its other attributes alone).

Its headline finding is that gains on the proxy metrics do not reliably translate into practical gains. Matryoshka SAEs sit slightly worse on the sparsity versus fidelity frontier yet score best on absorption and several disentanglement metrics in the typical L0 range of 40 to 200, while ReLU (L1) SAEs score worst on loss recovered.

**Dark matter.** Every SAE leaves an error term $\mathbf{x} - \hat{\mathbf{x}}$. Scaling Monosemanticity's Sonnet SAEs explained at least 65% of the variance, so up to about a third sat in the error. Gao et al.'s 16M-latent GPT-4 SAE scored 98.2% loss recovered, yet splicing it in gave the loss of a model trained with roughly 10% of GPT-4's compute. A statement such as 'the model uses feature X to do Y' is therefore a statement about the SAE's description plus whatever hides in the error; lesson 6's steering recipe keeps the error term for exactly this reason.

A decision guide that follows from the evidence:
- **Unsupervised discovery and hypothesis generation** (what is this layer tracking that I did not think to ask about?): an SAE is the right tool.
- **Detecting or steering a concept you can already label**: start with difference-in-means or a linear probe, then check whether an SAE latent adds anything.
- **Circuit-level claims**: use SAE-style dictionaries but test them causally (the circuit-tracing course).

Sparsity rewards absorbing a parent feature into its children, so SAE latents can have silent holes. Matryoshka and BatchTopK reduce the damage, but SAEs are not canonical units, and on labelled tasks simple baselines such as difference-in-means and linear probes usually match or beat them.

A latent with a clean label and a high autointerp score can still miss part of its concept. Before relying on one as a detector, measure its recall on labelled examples, and compare against a linear probe trained on the same data.

blocks.question: A 65k-latent SAE has a 'starts with E' latent that fires on almost every E-word except ' elephant', where an 'elephant' latent fires alone. What is the most likely explanation and fix?
options: The latent is dead on ' elephant'; add AuxK
Feature absorption: the elephant latent's decoder includes the 'starts with E' direction. Try a Matryoshka SAE, or check recall against a probe
Shrinkage from the L1 penalty; switch to TopK
The model does not know that elephant starts with E
blocks.explain: A hierarchy (elephant implies starts-with-E) lets sparsity merge the parent direction into the child latent, leaving a hole in the parent latent. Going wider or sparser tends to make it worse; nested Matryoshka losses penalise it. AuxK only helps latents that never fire.

blocks.question: Your team must flag customer messages that mention cancelling, and has 2,000 labelled examples. Which first approach does the evidence in this lesson support?
options: Search the SAE for a 'cancellation' latent and threshold it, since SAE latents are the model's true units
Train a much wider SAE until a perfect cancellation latent appears
Use raw model outputs only; internal activations cannot be probed
Train a linear probe or a difference-in-means direction on the raw activations, and use SAE latents only if they measurably add to it
blocks.explain: With labels available, Kantamneni et al. and AxBench found supervised baselines on raw activations match or beat SAE latents, especially under distribution shift. Wider SAEs absorb more, and SAE latents are not canonical units.

lessons.title: Build it yourself: train a TopK SAE on GPT-2, then use a released one

blocks.md:
Time to do it end to end. Part 1 trains a TopK SAE on the residual stream of GPT-2 small (the 124M-parameter model the prerequisite course rebuilt) entering block 6, which SAELens and Neuronpedia call `blocks.6.hook_resid_pre`. Part 2 loads a released SAE for the same site, reads its latents and steers with one.

Everything below ran for real on a laptop CPU with 2 threads: caching about 3.2 million tokens took about 12 minutes, and each SAE training run about 8 minutes. That is a toy budget. The released SAE in part 2 was trained on 300 million tokens, and Gao et al. trained their largest on 40 billion, so expect our numbers to be worse than published ones; the point is that every step of the pipeline is here.

**Step 1, cache activations.** Run the frozen model over text and save the vector at the chosen site for every token. Three details matter:
