- **Drop the first position.** Measured here, the residual stream at position 0 has a mean norm of 3028, against 80.2 at every other position. Gao et al. report the same order-of-magnitude outlier at most GPT-2 small layers (first positions act as attention resting places). Left in, a few such vectors would dominate the squared error. Gemma Scope also skips BOS, EOS and padding tokens.
- **Shuffle across documents.** Consecutive tokens of one document are highly correlated; a batch drawn from one document is a biased sample. Gemma Scope shuffles in buckets of about a million activations; with everything in memory we shuffle fully.
- **Normalise by one scalar.** Divide by $s = \sqrt{\mathbb{E}\|\mathbf{x}\|^2}$ so the mean squared norm is 1 (lesson 3). Here $s = 80.6$.

blocks.code:
import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("openai-community/gpt2")
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("openai-community/gpt2").eval()
model.transformer.h = model.transformer.h[:7]   # blocks 0..6 suffice
CTX = 128

def chunks(texts, per_doc=4):                    # BOS + 127 tokens each
    for t in texts:
        ids = tok(t)["input_ids"]
        for c in range(per_doc):
            piece = ids[c * (CTX - 1):(c + 1) * (CTX - 1)]
            if len(piece) == CTX - 1:
                yield [tok.bos_token_id] + piece

seqs = torch.tensor(list(chunks(texts)))
acts = []
with torch.no_grad():
    for i in range(0, len(seqs), 16):
        hs = model(seqs[i:i+16], output_hidden_states=True).hidden_states
        acts.append(hs[6][:, 1:].half())      # entering block 6; drop BOS
x = torch.cat(acts).reshape(-1, 768)
x = x[torch.randperm(len(x))]                 # shuffle across documents
scale = x[:100_000].float().pow(2).sum(-1).mean().sqrt()   # E||x/scale||^2 = 1
blocks.caption: Caching with Hugging Face transformers. hidden_states[6] is the input to block 6 (keep block 6 in the model: Hugging Face applies the final norm to the last entry). The real run used 9,600 Pile documents (NeelNanda/pile-10k), giving 3,223,387 tokens.

blocks.title: Residual-stream norm entering block 6 of GPT-2 small

scenes.caption: Measured on 25,381 cached sequences: mean norm 3028 at position 0 and 80.2 elsewhere, about 38 times larger.
Its square is over 1,000 times larger, so one BOS vector would outweigh a thousand ordinary tokens in the MSE. The SAE never sees position 0, and at use time we leave that position untouched.

blocks.md: **Step 2, the SAE.** A TopK SAE with $M = 16 \times 768 = 12{,}288$ latents and $k = 32$, trained with Adam (learning rate $4 \times 10^{-4}$) on batches of 2,048 tokens for 1,500 steps, about one pass over the cache. The recipe pieces all come from earlier lessons: the encoder starts as the decoder's transpose, decoder columns are renormalised to unit length after every step, $\mathbf{b}_{pre}$ starts at the data mean, and AuxK ($k_{aux} = 512$, $\alpha = 1/32$) kicks in for latents that have not fired in the last 200,000 tokens. That window is scaled down from the 10 million tokens Gao et al. use, because the whole run is only 3.1 million tokens.

blocks.code:
import torch.nn.functional as F
d, M, k, k_aux, alpha = 768, 16 * 768, 32, 512, 1 / 32
W_dec = F.normalize(torch.randn(d, M), dim=0)            # unit columns
W_enc = W_dec.T.clone()                                  # enc = dec^T
b_pre = (x[:100_000].float() / scale).mean(0)             # start at the data mean
b_enc = torch.zeros(M)
params = [p.requires_grad_() for p in (W_dec, W_enc, b_pre, b_enc)]
opt = torch.optim.Adam(params, lr=4e-4)
since_fired = torch.zeros(M)

for step in range(1500):
    xb = x[torch.randint(0, len(x), (2048,))].float() / scale
    pre = (xb - b_pre) @ W_enc.T + b_enc
    v, i = pre.topk(k, dim=-1)
    z = torch.zeros_like(pre).scatter(-1, i, F.relu(v))
    x_hat = z @ W_dec.T + b_pre
    loss = (xb - x_hat).pow(2).sum(-1).mean()
    since_fired += len(xb); since_fired[(z > 0).any(0)] = 0
    dead = since_fired > 200_000
    if dead.any():                                       # AuxK
        e = (xb - x_hat).detach()
        v, i = pre.masked_fill(~dead, -1e9).topk(min(k_aux, int(dead.sum())), -1)
        e_hat = torch.zeros_like(pre).scatter(-1, i, F.relu(v)) @ W_dec.T
        loss = loss + alpha * ((e - e_hat).pow(2).sum(-1) / e.pow(2).sum(-1)).mean()
    opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
    with torch.no_grad(): W_dec.data = F.normalize(W_dec.data, dim=0)
blocks.caption: The training loop as run (lightly condensed). The real script also logs FVU and the dead fraction every 50 steps. AuxK here is divided by the residual's squared norm, unlike lesson 4's formula. Gao et al. also project out the gradient parallel to each decoder column before Adam; we only renormalise.

blocks.title: One training step
blocks.code:
xb = x[batch].float() / scale
pre = (xb - b_pre) @ W_enc.T + b_enc
v, i = pre.topk(k, dim=-1)
z = zeros_like(pre).scatter(-1, i, relu(v))
x_hat = z @ W_dec.T + b_pre
loss = ((xb - x_hat) ** 2).sum(-1).mean()
since_fired += 2048
since_fired[(z > 0).any(0)] = 0
dead = since_fired > 200_000
if dead.any():
    e = (xb - x_hat).detach()
    z_dead = topk_of(pre, dead, k_aux)
    loss += alpha * norm_mse(e, z_dead @ W_dec.T)
loss.backward(); adam.step()
W_dec.data = normalize(W_dec.data, dim=0)

scenes.caption: Draw 2,048 random cached tokens and divide by the scale, so the batch mixes many documents.
Encode: centre, project to 12,288 pre-activations, keep the top 32 per token. Decode with the unit-norm columns.
The main loss is plain squared error: no sparsity penalty, because k already fixes L0 = 32.
Book-keeping for dead latents: reset the counter of every latent that fired in this batch.
AuxK: the top 512 dead latents try to explain the residual error e; their gradient pulls them back toward live data.
Update, then put every decoder column back on the unit sphere.

blocks.title: Training curves from the real runs

scenes.caption: Batch FVU of the k = 32 run every 250 steps: 0.7561 at the start, 0.2662 after about 1 million tokens, 0.1806 at the end. Still falling: a longer run would keep improving.
Dead fraction (no fire in the last 200,000 tokens) with a random encoder and no AuxK: it climbs steadily to 0.246 (24.6%). A latent that never wins a top-k slot gets no gradient.

Same random encoder with AuxK on: the dead fraction peaks near 20% (20.2% at 1.9M tokens, 19.8% at the 2.1M bar) and is pulled back to 10.4% as AuxK revives latents. With the transposed init (the k = 32 run) at most 0.01% was ever flagged dead.

blocks.code:
full = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("openai-community/gpt2").eval()
mode = {"m": None}

def splice(module, args):                  # runs just before block 6
    h = args[0]
    if mode["m"] is None: return None
    h = h.clone(); xs = h[:, 1:] / scale     # keep the BOS position as is
    if mode["m"] == "sae":  new = decode(encode(xs)) * scale
    if mode["m"] == "zero": new = torch.zeros_like(xs)
    if mode["m"] == "mean": new = (b_mean * scale).expand_as(xs)
    h[:, 1:] = new
    return (h,) + args[1:]

full.transformer.h[6].register_forward_pre_hook(splice)
ce = {}
with torch.no_grad():
    for m in [None, "sae", "zero", "mean"]:
        mode["m"] = m
        ce[m] = full(eval_ids, labels=eval_ids).loss.item()
print(ce)
blocks.caption: Splicing with a forward pre-hook on block 6 (abridged; the real script evaluates in batches of 16). Zero and mean ablation use the same hook, so all four losses come from one loop.

blocks.title: FVU against L0 from our three runs

scenes.caption: Held-out FVU at k = 16, 32 and 64 (same width, same 3.1M tokens): 0.225, 0.1863, 0.1618. The curve is a fit of FVU = A k^b through the three points (b = -0.24).
Delta LM loss falls with k too: 0.339, 0.2078 and 0.1433 nats. Each doubling of the active latents buys less, the same diminishing return as Gao et al.'s scaling law in lesson 6.

blocks.md:
**Part 2, use a released SAE.** SAELens hosts a registry of pretrained SAEs; `SAE.from_pretrained` downloads one by release name and SAE id. `gpt2-small-res-jb` holds Joseph Bloom's L1-trained residual-stream SAEs for every layer of GPT-2 small; the one at `blocks.6.hook_resid_pre` has 24,576 latents (32 times 768) and was trained on 300 million OpenWebText tokens.

Two practical traps. First, match the site exactly: same model, same layer, same hook point. Second, match the preprocessing: this SAE was trained on activations from TransformerLens (an interpretability library that reimplements GPT-2) with its centred-writing-weights option, which makes every vector written into the residual stream zero-mean, so every residual vector the SAE saw had zero mean across its 768 entries. Raw Hugging Face activations do not, so subtract each vector's mean first. Without that step the prompt below lit up 451 latents on 'The'; with it, 12.

blocks.code:
import torch
from sae_lens import SAE
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer
sae = SAE.from_pretrained(release="gpt2-small-res-jb",
                          sae_id="blocks.6.hook_resid_pre", device="cpu")
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("openai-community/gpt2")
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("openai-community/gpt2").eval()

text = "The Golden Gate Bridge is in San Francisco"
ids = torch.tensor([[tok.bos_token_id] + tok(text)["input_ids"]])
with torch.no_grad():
    h = model(ids, output_hidden_states=True).hidden_states[6]
    f = sae.encode(h - h.mean(-1, keepdim=True))[0]     # [tokens, 24576]
for p in range(1, ids.shape[1]):
    v, i = f[p].topk(3)
    print(repr(tok.decode(ids[0, p])), i.tolist(), v.round(decimals=1).tolist(),
          "L0", int((f[p] > 0).sum()))

Neuronpedia's labels for these latents (open gpt2-small/6-res-jb/<index>): 17575 'Golden State' or 'the Golden Gate Bridge', 5395 'physical structures like bridges', 1683 'references to San Francisco'.
13362 is labelled 'cities starting with San' (San Jose, San Diego, San Antonio) and fires on ' San' before the model has seen Francisco: it reads the token, not the city.
L0 per token is 12 to 63 latents, far from the 32 a TopK SAE would force: this is an L1 SAE, so sparsity varies by token.

blocks.md:
Finally, steer with latent 5,395 using lesson 6's recipe: encode, then add $(c - f_i)\,\mathbf{d}_i$ at every position after BOS, generated tokens included, so the SAE's error term is kept. Its logit effect (lesson 5, computed through the final LayerNorm gain) promotes 'port', 'bridge', ' bridges', ' bridge' and ' Strait', so the hypothesis is 'pushes the model to talk about bridges'.

Greedy continuations of 'My favourite place to visit is':
- clean: 'the beach. It's a beautiful place to spend a day...'
- clamped to 50 (about 1.1 times its largest observed activation): 'the one between the Thames and the Thames. This is the first bridge over the river.'

And 'The best way to get across the river is': clean 'to go to the river'; clamped to 50 'to use the bridge over the St. George. The bridge over the bridge over the bridge'. The name passes the causal test. The usable range is narrow, though: at 100 or more both prompts collapse into 'over to to to...'. AxBench tunes this strength for every method, and SAE latents still trailed prompting and difference-in-means there.

blocks.code:
LATENT, state = 5395, {"c": None}

def clamp(module, args):            # x' = x + (c - f_i) d_i, error kept
    if state["c"] is None:
        return None
    h = args[0].clone()
    centred = h - h.mean(-1, keepdim=True)
    f_i = sae.encode(centred)[..., LATENT:LATENT + 1]
    delta = (state["c"] - f_i) * sae.W_dec[LATENT]
    s = 1 if h.shape[1] > 1 else 0  # prompt: skip BOS; cached step: 1 token
    h[:, s:] += delta[:, s:]
    return (h,) + args[1:]

model.transformer.h[6].register_forward_pre_hook(clamp)
p = torch.tensor([[tok.bos_token_id] + tok("My favourite place to visit is")["input_ids"]])
for c in [None, 50.0]:
    state["c"] = c
    with torch.no_grad():
        out = model.generate(p, max_new_tokens=20, do_sample=False,
                             pad_token_id=tok.eos_token_id)
    print(c, repr(tok.decode(out[0, 1:])))
blocks.caption: Clamping as a forward pre-hook. After the prompt, generate feeds one new token per call (KV cache), so the hook must steer that token too; skipping position 0 there would leave every generated token unsteered. LayerNorm removes the mean, so adding d_i to the uncentred vector is fine.

blocks.md: A working SAE pipeline is: cache a site with BOS dropped, shuffle, normalise by one scalar, train with transposed init and unit decoder columns (plus AuxK at scale), then judge it by L0, FVU and delta LM loss from splicing. A released SAE plus Neuronpedia gets you to reading and steering in a few lines.

Our 3-million-token runs are far below real budgets, so their numbers are illustrative of the pipeline, not of what TopK SAEs can do. Also check that a released SAE's site, model and preprocessing match yours exactly: an SAE trained on resid_pre of layer 6 is meaningless on layer 7 or on another model.

blocks.question: You forget to drop position 0 when caching GPT-2 small activations at this site. What is the most likely symptom?
options: Many latents end up dedicated to the few huge BOS vectors, and FVU is dominated by them, while ordinary tokens reconstruct poorly
Nothing: the SAE averages over tokens, so one position cannot matter
The SAE gets more dead latents because BOS vectors are small
Training becomes faster because the BOS vectors are easy
blocks.explain: Position 0's norm here is about 38 times the others, so its squared error is over 1,000 times larger. Unnormalised, those vectors dominate the loss and the scale estimate. That is why caches skip BOS, EOS and padding.

blocks.question: Your SAE has FVU 0.19 and loss recovered 97.9% (zero ablation) at this residual site. Which extra number best tells you whether it is good enough to splice into the model for an analysis?
options: Its L0, because sparser is always better
The number of latents
Delta LM loss in nats (here about 0.2), compared with what your analysis can tolerate
The decoder norms
blocks.explain: Zero-ablating the residual stream is so destructive that loss recovered looks excellent for almost any SAE. Delta LM loss says directly how much worse the spliced model predicts text; 0.2 nats is a large degradation.
